La plupart des gens que j'ai contactés é: Most of the people I contacted were very enthusiastic about discussing the rise of English in Morocco and their relationship to French. It gave me access to a wealth of information and a variety of perspectives, and it also showed me how much the subject resonates in Moroccan society. However, that enthusiasm also posed a challenge in the writing: the diversity of the responses and the many aspects raised made the subject much broader than I had anticipated. I had to narrow my focus to avoid spreading myself too thin.
J'ai finalement choisi de me concentrer: In the end, I chose to focus solely on the social and cultural aspects of the subject. Although many other angles were just as interesting, such as the economic or political aspects, the social and cultural dimensions seemed to me the ones that touched daily life most directly.
Un autre défi que j'ai rencontré était l: Another challenge I faced had to do with my own perceptions and experiences. Having grown up in Morocco, some things that may seem peculiar or intriguing to other people seemed normal to me. I had to step back and, in discussion with the team, rethink certain things I took for granted and adopt a more neutral perspective to make sure my story was accessible and relevant to readers who haven’t lived in the same country.
<strong>Alors que s'ouvre aujourd'hui le: As the Francophonie Summit opens today in Paris, La Converse looked at the use of French in Morocco, especially in the big cities. Casablanca is not immune to a recent linguistic phenomenon: long dominant in Morocco, the French language is losing its lustre to English, adopted by a generation that is proud of its culture, open to the world and eager to break free from post-colonial ties.
Casablanca, fin septembre. Dans un centr: Casablanca, late September. In a cultural centre, young people attend a screening of Quebec short films with English subtitles, then start a discussion… in English. It’s a scene that would have seemed implausible less than ten years ago, in a city where French was long the preferred language of a certain cultural milieu.
Comprendre l’évolution des langues étran: Understanding the evolution of foreign languages in Morocco is impossible without first looking at the country’s linguistic landscape. Darija, Moroccan Arabic, is used in everyday life, with borrowings from several languages, including Tamazight, the Indigenous language of Morocco. It is distinct from literary Arabic, the written and official language, used in speeches, the press and education, and shared by all Arabic-speaking countries.
Un perpétuel débat existe dans la sociét: A perpetual debate runs through Moroccan society: some argue for recognizing darija as a language in its own right, given its marked differences from classical Arabic, while others fear that doing so would weaken the use of literary Arabic, the language of education, of the Muslim religion and of official texts.
Quant au français, près de 70 ans après: As for French, nearly 70 years after Morocco’s independence, it remains very present in many spheres of society, even though it has never had the status of an official language. It is one of the languages of public administration, education and the media, among others. But for about ten years now, English has become much more visible and audible in Morocco, on social media, in bookstores and on café terraces.
Cette forte émergence de l’anglais s’acc: This strong emergence of English goes hand in hand with a certain distancing from the French language, closely tied to a thirst to revive and proudly claim Moroccan culture. For Ibtissam Ghazoui, cultural manager at the American arts centre in Casablanca, it’s not about replacing one foreign language with another, but about breaking away from a culture and a language that “was imposed on us, whereas English is a language we chose.”
« Valoriser et célébrer notre culture ma: “Valuing and celebrating our Moroccan culture has allowed us to realize what colonization did to us,” she adds. “Before, speaking French was a symbol of social and intellectual status. That’s no longer the case today.”
Dans un pays où l'offre culturelle local: In a country where local cultural offerings are slim, foreign cultural diplomacy fills the void. The American arts centre, open for less than two years, is quickly establishing itself as the city’s leading cultural space.
Contrairement aux instituts culturels fr: Unlike at the French cultural institutes, people here speak darija. Dance and writing workshops are offered in darija and English. Most participants are teenagers who arrive on skateboards from working-class neighbourhoods of Casablanca such as Hay Mohammadi, Sidi Moumen or Ain Sebaa.
Diplômée en politique et gestion culture: A graduate in cultural policy and management, Ibtissam notes that many artists want to develop Moroccan culture rather than try their luck abroad, as a generation of French-speaking North African authors and musicians did when they aspired to success in France. “Recently, there has been a very interesting awakening to our own identity,” she says.

C’est notamment le cas pour Khtek. À 29: That is especially true for Khtek. At 29, the rapper has a natural self-assurance that never tips into arrogance. Like many Moroccans of her generation, her sentences mix up to three languages at once. She meets us at a café in old Maarif, a neighbourhood in central Casablanca. Houda, her real name, chose her stage name, which means “Your sister,” to reclaim an expression that is all too often used pejoratively in the macho world of rap.
La jeune femme a grandi dans une famille: The young woman grew up in a middle-class family that encouraged her to read and write in French. “At home, it was an important language to learn,” she says. As a teenager, this lover of French-language literature devoured books, from Milan Kundera to Amin Maalouf. Then she started getting interested in American music and film. “I started to love English. I wrote letters to Kurt Cobain in my diary. I learned songs by heart. I printed out the lyrics and tried to understand what they meant. That’s how my level improved.”
Later, the language fed her passion. “It’s thanks to English that I rap today,” she says. “It’s by discovering American hip-hop and being able to understand that culture that I rap today. The first song that inspired me was ‘Suicidal Thoughts’ by Notorious B.I.G. If I didn’t speak English, that song surely would never have captivated and moved me so much.”
Aujourd’hui, elle est consciente du priv: Today, she is aware of the privilege of having learned French outside public school, at home or through private lessons. “In Morocco, learning French is a privilege because the level of French in public schools is low.”
Pour beaucoup de Marocains natifs numéri: For many digital-native Moroccans, English is easier to master than French or literary Arabic. It also opens up more of the world, and the internet and social media have accelerated this enthusiasm.
Entissar, Maroco-irakienne de 36 ans, es: Entissar, a 36-year-old Moroccan-Iraqi woman, is calm and radiant, and gives off a natural serenity. She remembers getting close to English well before the internet arrived in Morocco. At 10, she stumbled upon an old English book at her aunt’s house and learned a few words. “Back then, we had neither internet nor cell phones. There was nothing to do, so we kept ourselves busy as best we could.”
À l’adolescence, sa famille vit à Bagdad: As a teenager, her family lived in Baghdad for two years. That’s where she took her first English classes at school. “The first things I liked about English is that common nouns have no gender. There’s no masculine or feminine. It was a revelation for me.”
Mais si l’envie d’utiliser davantage l’a: But while the desire to use more English in Morocco is increasingly felt, especially among young people, it doesn’t necessarily translate on the ground, particularly in education. Morocco is still home to the second-largest network, after Lebanon, of the Agency for French Education Abroad (AEFE). These schools, located around the world, offer teaching that follows the French education system. In Montréal, for example, the Collège international Marie-de-France and the Collège Stanislas fall under the AEFE.
Au Maroc, la <l1>majorité</l1> des élève: In Morocco, the <l1>majority</l1> of students enrolled in these schools are Moroccan nationals or dual citizens. Among them, Driss did all of his schooling at a French school in Marrakech. He is one of those young Moroccans, born to Moroccan parents and living in Morocco, who speak only French at school and at home.
Le jeune homme au français impeccable vi: The young man, whose French is impeccable, has just turned 18. Composed, he gives off a serenity and maturity rare for his age. This fall, he is starting a program taught entirely in English at Al Akhawayn University in Ifrane. “I didn’t have a lot of trouble switching languages because my English isn’t bad.” It’s not so much in class that Driss has trouble communicating, but with the rest of his classmates, most of whom speak darija. “That’s where I struggle more, because my Arabic isn’t very good,” he says.

Dans les écoles privées marocaines, géné: In Moroccan private schools, generally, half of the classes are taught in Arabic and the other half in French. In the Moroccan public education system, French is taught more than English. But the level remains fairly low. Rajae, 35, teaches French to all ages. Her youngest students are often children who attend public schools and whose parents want to give them extra French instruction.
Pour ce qui est des adolescents, Rajae a: As for teenagers, Rajae is used to hearing them say they don’t want to learn the language of the colonizer. “When I see that they’re not interested and I ask them why they don’t make an effort to learn when they’re in French class, they answer: anyway, I’m only here because I have to be, but what I want is to learn English. I’m only here to pass my exams.”
Les adultes en revanche semblent beaucou: Adults, on the other hand, seem much more invested in learning, to advance professionally and move up the ladder. “Let’s not kid ourselves,” says Rajae. “We’re in Morocco. It’s true that more and more people speak English here, but we’re still very far from becoming a country where English is the first foreign language. In the meantime, you need to secure your professional future.”
Début 2024, sur un plateau radio de l’ém: In early 2024, on the set of the French radio show Planète Rap, relocated to Casablanca, Khtek improvised a track. She flipped off the camera filming the scene while rapping: “F**k the colonizers, hna kandwiw b’darija” [F**k the colonizers, here we speak darija, Editor’s note].
Bien qu’elle conserve une affinité pour: Although she retains an affinity for the French language, her interest in decolonial thought has led her to question its use in public space. “When a Moroccan doesn’t make the effort to speak darija and wants to impose on other Moroccans to speak French in their own country, to me, that’s a colonialist approach. We socially exclude people who have a strong accent in French or who don’t master the language.”
Une observation que confirme Entissar. «: Entissar confirms this observation. “From my experience, French is synonymous with classism. Even at the level of services [hotels, shops, etc.], when you speak darija, they don’t treat you the same way as if you speak French. I do speak French, but if I were given the choice, I would rather speak another language.”
Selon Khtek, le rejet de la langue franç: According to Khtek, rejecting the French language is “an unconscious rebellion of the new generation.” She believes that the existence of a French-speaking elite in Morocco is “damage done by colonialism.” In Morocco, she sometimes gets corrected when she speaks French. In a society where you can be looked down on for not mastering a foreign language that is, moreover, poorly taught in public schools, Khtek is delighted to see young people from working-class neighbourhoods learning English through music or the internet.
« Lorsqu’une personne plus âgée veut leu: “When an older person wants to force them to speak French, and they answer that they speak English and not French, I find that powerful. (...) It’s a counterattack, because it’s violence to force people to speak a language they never had the chance to learn and to consider them worthless because of it,” says Khtek.
Avancer l’argument de la colonisation po: Invoking colonization to defend a linguistic choice may seem inconsistent when the alternative is the language of the British and the Americans. But for Khtek, “since English is accessible, I have no problem with that language. You can learn it on your own, easily, just on social media and by watching YouTube, and knowing it isn’t classist. Even though England colonized many countries around the world, we have a different relationship to this language.”
Une langue plus accessible, précise-t-el: A more accessible language, she adds: “It’s acceptable to have an accent. All over the world, people speak English with different accents. And it’s easier to learn.”
L’Espagne a également colonisé le nord e: Spain also colonized the north and south of Morocco, but France’s influence on Moroccan society is more “toxic,” according to the rapper. A toxicity that produces rejection: “You can even see it in soccer. A Moroccan who has no idea what decolonial thought is, who has never read Frantz Fanon, watching a soccer match between Spain and France, will cheer for Spain. We literally savour France’s defeat.”
Oussama, 31 ans, préfère avancer des arg: Oussama, 31, prefers to make logical arguments rather than emotional ones. For this French teacher, the argument of colonization shouldn’t interfere with the choice of whether or not to communicate in this language. “Yes, it was the language of the colonizer, but if we have to make choices, we shouldn’t base them on arguments of hatred, even if it’s part of our history and we don’t like what happened. We have to be reasonable now, and we’re in the 21st century. We don’t forget the past, but we act logically, thinking about things reasonably.”
Parfois, un débat s’installe dans sa cla: Sometimes a debate breaks out in his class, with his adult students: “a lot of people don’t like French, and they make that argument. Me, for example, I would be in favour of using English more, because it’s a simple language, more open, and it gives access to many more countries, for studies or for work. We have to put forward logical arguments rather than think about this question emotionally.”

The world in its original version
Avant l’arrivée d’internet au Maroc, l’a: Before the internet arrived in Morocco, the foreign art and culture Moroccans consumed came mainly from Egypt or France. As for English-language films, literature and music, Moroccans discovered them mostly through French channels, where the works were dubbed or translated. What caused a sensation in France also found its place in Morocco, but often with a delay, limiting Moroccans’ exposure to English-language culture in all its diversity.
L'accès direct aux cultures anglophones: Direct access to English-language cultures through the internet has changed consumption habits and forced several sectors to adapt their offerings to the new expectations of the Moroccan public. American films in movie theatres were, until very recently, available only in French. Today, several screenings in the original version with French subtitles are available every day.
Du côté des médias, certaines rédactions: In the media, some newsrooms now have English-language teams. The news sites Hespress and TelQuel have English versions of their websites. The public channel Al Aoula is reportedly developing an English-language news channel.
Du côté de la lecture, le <em>Carrefour: When it comes to reading, Carrefour des Livres has long been the go-to French-language bookstore in Casablanca. Today, nearly half of its shelves hold books in English, ranging from classics to the most recent novels and self-help books. Ten years ago, you couldn’t find a single book in English in Morocco, but today several bookstores and distributors import them.
Pour Yacine Retnani, propriétaire du <em: For Yacine Retnani, owner of Carrefour des Livres, the trigger was first financial. With more competition, notably from online bookstores, and the Covid crisis, he had to adapt and find a way to survive. “English and Arabic saved us, because if we had clung to our French-speaking customers who were disappearing one by one or going elsewhere, we would have closed.”
Mariam Benabdellah, âgée de 27 ans, est: Mariam Benabdellah, 27, is delighted to see a young clientele at Carrefour des Livres. The bookseller always has a big, warm smile. She is welcoming and gives visitors the time and space to wander through the store. Young people now make up nearly 80% of her customers. “They buy several books at a time, they’re willing to spend up to 500 dirhams (about 70 dollars) on books.” ***
La rentrée littéraire de la librairie es: The bookstore’s fall literary season has now been replaced by BookTok**. It was in fact thanks to the store’s recently created TikTok account that this English-speaking clientele discovered it. “We didn’t lose French-speaking readers for English-speaking ones, but we found a new clientele that didn’t know us,” says Yacine Retnani. “We’ve been on the same street for 40 years and now people walk in who didn’t know the bookstore existed, because it was a labelled French-language bookstore.”
Pour Rajae, « parler plusieurs langues o: For Rajae, “speaking several languages opens a lot of doors. It also opens your mind and your way of thinking. By learning a language, you discover another culture.” Her command of French made it easier for her to get a job, while her command of English allowed her to study abroad.
Cette ouverture sur le monde, Yacine Ret: Yacine Retnani encourages this openness to the world. Besides owning a bookstore, he is also the director of the publishing house La Croisée des Chemins. “It was totally logical and consistent for me to introduce Moroccan authors who write very good texts in English to young people who will read in English and follow social media trends.” The first English-language novel published by La Croisée des Chemins is The House on Butterfly Street, by Mhani Alaoui. Since then, the publisher has received about fifteen manuscripts in English and plans to publish other English-speaking Moroccan talents.
De quoi, sans doute, réjouir Khtek. « La: That is sure to please Khtek. “The best language in the world for me is darija, even though many people consider it a dialect and not a language,” she concludes. What is certain is that English is taking up more space in Morocco. But when it comes to French, there seem to be as many opinions as there are Moroccans. In the meantime, young people are perfecting their skill at juggling between languages, often unconsciously, depending on the context.
